title: Sweat Chloride and CA 19-9: Cut-offs That Do Not Rule Out
summary: Learn the current sweat chloride bands for cystic fibrosis, how newborn screening with immunoreactive trypsinogen leads to a sweat test, and why a normal CA 19-9 cannot rule out pancreatic cancer in Lewis-negative patients.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 23 Hit 10 (sweat chloride for cystic fibrosis; newborn screening starts with IRT, then CFTR genetics), Hit 12 (CA 19-9 reference 0–37 U/mL; >100 U/mL highly specific; Lewis-negative patients) and Trap 4 (a normal CA 19-9 does not rule out pancreatic adenocarcinoma). Checked against Pagaduan 2018, the Croatian national sweat test guidelines (Leniček Krleža 2022), the CF Foundation newborn screening guideline (McGarry 2025), Farrell 2020, Guo 2017 and Liu 2025 (all Europe PMC full text) and Ballehaninna 2012 (read via a page-fetch tool). The CF Foundation 2017 diagnostic guideline itself is not open access and was not read; its bands are taught as summarised by Pagaduan 2018 and the Croatian guidelines. Qualified: the sources give ≥60 mmol/L as consistent with CF and 30–59 mmol/L as intermediate (not the Number Vault’s 50–60 “suggestive”), and no source read states a two-occasion requirement (register flag rv-sweat-cl-bands-2017); Lewis-negative patients usually make little or no CA 19-9, but some Lewis-negative cancer patients have been reported with raised levels (register flag rv-ca199-lewis-not-absolute). Not taught: the 50–60 mmol/L band and the other Number Vault rows.

objectives: Interpret a sweat chloride result using the normal, intermediate and elevated bands, and state why conductivity cannot make the diagnosis.
Describe the newborn screening sequence for cystic fibrosis (IRT, CFTR variant testing, sweat test) and why a positive screen is not a diagnosis.
Explain why a normal CA 19-9 cannot exclude pancreatic cancer and which conditions raise CA 19-9 without cancer.

scenes.title: Two reassuring numbers?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two reports reach the same chemistry bench. (1) A 3-month-old referred after a positive cystic fibrosis newborn screen (elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen, one CF-causing CFTR variant) has a sweat chloride of 42 mmol/L. (2) A 68-year-old with weight loss and a pancreatic mass on imaging has a serum CA 19-9 that is undetectable. Question token: “CF ruled out? Cancer ruled out?”

cues.text: Two reports reach the bench. A three-month-old with a positive newborn screen for cystic fibrosis has a sweat chloride of forty-two millimoles per litre.
A sixty-eight-year-old with a pancreatic mass on imaging has a CA 19-9 that is undetectable.
Both numbers look reassuring. Is cystic fibrosis ruled out? Is cancer ruled out?

props.label: CF ruled out? Cancer ruled out?

scenes.title: Reading a sweat chloride
scenes.altText: Schematic forearm with a sweat collector. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disease of the CFTR protein, which regulates electrolyte transport across epithelial membranes; CFTR dysfunction raises the chloride concentration in sweat. Method card: sweating stimulated by pilocarpine iontophoresis, sweat collected, chloride measured by colorimetry, coulometry or ion-selective electrode; conductivity is a screening method, not acceptable as a reference method for diagnosis. Interpretation bar (CF Foundation 2017, as summarised by the sources): ≤29 mmol/L normal (CF unlikely), 30–59 mmol/L intermediate (borderline), ≥60 mmol/L elevated (consistent with CF). Note: the intermediate range was lowered from 40–59 to 30–59 mmol/L for people over 6 months.

cues.text: Cystic fibrosis is a recessive disease of CFTR, a membrane protein that moves chloride across epithelia. When CFTR fails, sweat chloride rises.
Sweating is stimulated with pilocarpine iontophoresis, the sweat is collected, and chloride itself is measured. Conductivity reads all sweat anions, so it can screen but cannot make the diagnosis.
Read chloride on three bands: twenty-nine or below is normal, thirty to fifty-nine is intermediate, and sixty or above is consistent with cystic fibrosis.
The 2017 Cystic Fibrosis Foundation guideline lowered the bottom of the intermediate band from forty to thirty.

scenes.title: From newborn screen to diagnosis
scenes.altText: Flow diagram. Step 1: immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT), a pancreatic enzyme precursor, measured on the dried blood spot; usually elevated in infants with CF, but also raised in some carriers and for reasons unrelated to CF (premature or traumatic birth, perinatal stress, ancestry). Step 2: elevated IRT reflexes to a CFTR variant panel; a CFTR sequencing tier after the panel improves specificity and positive predictive value. Step 3: screen-positive infants are referred for a sweat test (recommended from about 2 weeks of age and >2 kg). Caution card: newborn screening is a screening test, not a diagnosis, and does not detect every case; symptoms or family history justify a sweat test even after a normal screen. Diagnosis card: clinical suspicion (symptoms, positive screen or family history) plus evidence of CFTR dysfunction (raised sweat chloride), or two CF-causing CFTR variants.

cues.text: Newborn screening starts with immunoreactive trypsinogen, a pancreatic enzyme precursor measured on the blood spot. It is usually raised in babies with cystic fibrosis, but also in some carriers and after premature or stressful births.

So a raised trypsinogen reflexes to a CFTR variant panel, and some programmes add gene sequencing to improve specificity. Screen-positive babies are then sent for a sweat test, from about two weeks of age.
A newborn screen is a screen, not a diagnosis, and it misses some cases. A child with symptoms or a family history still needs a sweat test after a normal screen.

The diagnosis needs clinical suspicion plus proof of CFTR dysfunction, usually a raised sweat chloride. Two clearly disease-causing CFTR variants can also confirm it. An intermediate result calls for genetic analysis and follow-up.

scenes.title: CA 19-9 and the Lewis licence
scenes.altText: Schematic biosynthesis: precursor chain → sialylation → fucose added by the Lewis-gene enzyme FUT3 (α-1,4-fucosyltransferase) → CA 19-9 (sialyl Lewis a). Lewis a−b− people (about 5–10%; 9.8% in a Chinese cohort, whose Lewis-null members had undetectable CA 19-9) lack this enzyme activity and make little or none. Numbers card (Ballehaninna 2012): upper limit of normal 37 U/mL; in symptomatic patients sensitivity 79–81%, specificity 82–90%; raising the cut-off to 100 U/mL raised specificity to 98% but lowered sensitivity to 68%. False-elevation card: obstructive jaundice (10–60% false positivity), pancreatitis and other benign disease; recheck after biliary drainage. Screening card: PPV 0.5–0.9% in asymptomatic people, so not a screening test. Hook answers: (1) 42 mmol/L is intermediate, not normal: genetic analysis and follow-up; (2) undetectable CA 19-9 does not exclude cancer: possible Lewis-negative patient.

cues.text: CA 19-9 is sialyl Lewis a. The last step needs the Lewis enzyme, FUT3. About five to ten percent of people are Lewis negative, lack it, and make little or no CA 19-9.
The usual upper limit is thirty-seven units per millilitre. Above one hundred, specificity reaches about ninety-eight percent in one review, but sensitivity drops.

Obstructive jaundice, pancreatitis and other benign disease raise it too, so recheck after biliary drainage. And in people without symptoms the positive predictive value is under one percent: it is not a screening test.
Back to the hook. Forty-two is intermediate, so the infant needs genetic analysis and follow-up. The undetectable CA 19-9 may simply mean a Lewis-negative patient: cancer is not excluded.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal CA 19-9 rules out pancreatic cancer” (✓ Lewis-negative people make little or none; sensitivity is only about 80%); “CA 19-9 above 37 in a jaundiced patient means cancer” (✓ biliary obstruction and benign disease raise it; recheck after drainage); “A positive newborn screen means CF” (✓ IRT also rises in carriers and stressed or premature babies; the sweat test confirms).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal CA 19-9 rules out pancreatic cancer. No: Lewis-negative patients make little or none, and even in others sensitivity is only about eighty percent.
Trap two: a raised CA 19-9 in a jaundiced patient means cancer. No: biliary obstruction alone raises it. Recheck after drainage.
Trap three: a positive newborn screen means cystic fibrosis. No: trypsinogen also rises in carriers and stressed babies. The sweat test confirms.

props.title: ✗ “High CA 19-9 + jaundice = cancer.”
lines: ✓ Obstruction raises it; recheck after drainage

scenes.title: Sixty salty, thirty think, Lewis licence
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SIXTY is SALTY (≥60 mmol/L consistent with CF), THIRTY means THINK (30–59 intermediate, work it up); CA 19-9 needs a LEWIS LICENCE — no FUT3, no marker.” Tokens: ≥60 salty · 30–59 think · no Lewis, no CA 19-9. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: sixty is salty, thirty means think. Sixty or more fits cystic fibrosis; thirty to fifty-nine needs work-up. And CA 19-9 needs a Lewis licence: no Lewis enzyme, no marker.
Where it breaks: the bands apply to measured chloride, not conductivity; a salty sweat still needs clinical suspicion; and some Lewis-negative cancer patients have been reported with raised CA 19-9.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Sweat chloride: ≤29 normal · 30–59 intermediate · ≥60 consistent with CF · newborn screen ≠ diagnosis”, “CA 19-9: normal < 37 U/mL · Lewis-negative make little or none · jaundice raises it · not a screening test”.

cues.text: A sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or more supports cystic fibrosis only alongside clinical suspicion, 30 to 59 is intermediate and needs work-up, a positive newborn screen is not a diagnosis, and a normal CA 19-9 cannot rule out pancreatic cancer because Lewis-negative people make little or none.

props.label: Sweat Cl: ≤29 normal · 30–59 intermediate · ≥60 CF · screen ≠ diagnosis
CA 19-9: < 37 normal · Lewis − make none · jaundice raises · no screening

explanation.what: Plain language: in cystic fibrosis the sweat is too salty, so the lab measures chloride in sweat; a newborn blood-spot test only flags babies who need that sweat test. CA 19-9 is a sugar marker that some people genetically cannot make, so a normal value never clears a patient of pancreatic cancer. Scientific terms: cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), pilocarpine iontophoresis, sweat chloride, conductivity (NaCl equivalents), immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT), CFTR variant panel, CFTR-related metabolic syndrome / CF screen positive inconclusive diagnosis (CRMS/CFSPID), carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (sialyl Lewis a), FUT3 (α-1,4-fucosyltransferase), Lewis a−b− phenotype, positive predictive value.
explanation.why: CFTR dysfunction raises sweat chloride, so measured chloride (not total anions) reflects CFTR function. IRT is raised by CF but also by carrier status and perinatal stress, so it is a first tier only. CA 19-9 synthesis needs the Lewis-gene fucosyltransferase; people without it make little or none, and cholestasis and benign pancreatobiliary disease raise it.
explanation.measure: Sweat chloride (colorimetry, coulometry, ion-selective electrode): ≤29 mmol/L normal, 30–59 intermediate, ≥60 elevated; conductivity is screening only; test from about 2 weeks of age and >2 kg. Newborn screening: IRT → CFTR variant panel (± sequencing) → sweat test. CA 19-9: upper limit 37 U/mL; symptomatic sensitivity 79–81%, specificity 82–90%; at 100 U/mL specificity about 98%, sensitivity about 68%; screening PPV 0.5–0.9%.
explanation.differs: Intermediate (30–59) vs elevated (≥60) sweat chloride; screen-positive vs diagnosed CF; chloride vs conductivity; Lewis-positive vs Lewis-negative CA 19-9 producers; benign obstruction (falls after drainage) vs malignancy.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a sweat chloride value, name the first newborn screening analyte and why it is not specific, reject “normal CA 19-9 rules out cancer”, or explain an undetectable CA 19-9 by the Lewis phenotype.

comparisons.distinguisher: The 60 mmol/L line, applied to measured chloride in a person with clinical suspicion.

comparisons.title: CA 19-9 in Lewis-positive vs Lewis-negative patients
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the Lewis fucosyltransferase can complete the antigen.

mnemonic.text: SIXTY is SALTY (≥60 mmol/L consistent with CF), THIRTY means THINK (30–59 intermediate, work it up); CA 19-9 needs a LEWIS LICENCE — no FUT3, no marker.
mnemonic.explanation: Anchors the two sweat chloride thresholds and the genetic reason CA 19-9 can be falsely low.
mnemonic.limitation: The bands apply to measured chloride, not conductivity; a raised sweat chloride still needs clinical suspicion for diagnosis; some Lewis-negative cancer patients have been reported with raised CA 19-9.

CA 19-9 sensitivity and specificity figures come from one review and vary by cohort and assay.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old referred after a positive cystic fibrosis newborn screen has a sweat chloride of 45 mmol/L measured by coulometry. How should this result be classified?

options.text: Intermediate: cystic fibrosis is not excluded and CFTR genetic analysis and follow-up are needed
options.rationale: Correct. 30–59 mmol/L is the intermediate range in the 2017 CF Foundation bands.
Incorrect. Normal is 29 mmol/L or below; the intermediate range was lowered to start at 30 mmol/L.
Incorrect. A result consistent with CF is 60 mmol/L or above.

options.text: Uninterpretable, because sweat tests cannot be done before 6 months
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sweat testing is recommended from about 2 weeks of age in a term infant over 2 kg.

questions.stem: A patient with a biopsy-proven pancreatic adenocarcinoma has a CA 19-9 below the assay’s detection limit. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Lewis a−b− phenotype: no FUT3 activity to complete the CA 19-9 antigen
options.rationale: Correct. CA 19-9 is sialyl Lewis a, and Lewis-negative people make little or none.
Incorrect. Biliary obstruction RAISES CA 19-9, causing false positives.
Incorrect. Without FUT2, Lewis a is not converted to Lewis b, and CA 19-9 tends to be higher, not absent.

options.text: CA 19-9 is never produced by pancreatic cancers
options.rationale: Incorrect. CA 19-9 is raised in most symptomatic patients with pancreatic cancer (sensitivity about 79–81% in one review).

questions.stem: Which statement about immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) in cystic fibrosis newborn screening is correct?

options.text: It is usually raised in infants with CF but also in some carriers and stressed or premature infants, so a raised IRT leads to CFTR testing and a sweat test
options.rationale: Correct. IRT is the first tier; it is not specific, and screen-positive infants need a sweat test.

options.text: A raised IRT is diagnostic of CF
options.rationale: Incorrect. Newborn screening is a screening test, not a diagnostic test.

options.text: A normal IRT excludes CF even in a child with typical symptoms
options.rationale: Incorrect. Screening misses some cases; symptomatic children still need a sweat test.

options.text: IRT is measured in sweat collected by pilocarpine iontophoresis
options.rationale: Incorrect. IRT is a pancreatic enzyme precursor measured in the dried blood spot.

claims.text: Sweat chloride ≤29 mmol/L normal, 30–59 intermediate, ≥60 consistent with CF; intermediate range lowered from 40–59 to 30–59 in 2017.
claims.note: The 2017 CF Foundation guideline itself was not read (not open access); bands taken from the two sources that cite it.

claims.text: CFTR dysfunction raises sweat chloride; pilocarpine iontophoresis; chloride by colorimetry, coulometry or ISE; conductivity not acceptable for diagnosis; test from about 2 weeks and >2 kg.
CF diagnosis = clinical suspicion plus CFTR dysfunction, or two CF-causing variants; intermediate results need genetic analysis and follow-up.

Newborn screening: IRT first, usually high in CF but also in carriers and stressed or premature infants; CFTR variant panel ± sequencing (improves specificity); sweat test confirms; screening misses some cases.
CA 19-9 is sialyl Lewis a, completed by FUT3; Lewis a−b− people (about 5–10%) make little or none, so a normal value cannot exclude cancer; some Lewis-negative cancer patients have raised levels.

CA 19-9 normal <37 U/mL; symptomatic sensitivity 79–81%, specificity 82–90%; at 100 U/mL specificity ~98%, sensitivity ~68%; obstructive jaundice and benign disease raise it; recheck after drainage; screening PPV 0.5–0.9%.
Reviewer: sweat chloride >60 mmol/L “on two occasions” is diagnostic, and 50–60 mmol/L is “suggestive”; IRT has “high sensitivity”.
claims.note: No source read states a two-occasion requirement; the sources give 30–59 as intermediate; IRT sensitivity was not quantified in the sources read. Not taught as stated.

claims.text: Scenarios invented; sweat collector and glycan pathway drawn schematically.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 23 Hit 10 says sweat chloride >60 mmol/L “on two occasions” is diagnostic, and the Number Vault gives 50–60 mmol/L as suggestive. Pagaduan 2018 and the Croatian national guidelines (citing CF Foundation 2017) give ≥60 mmol/L as consistent with CF, 30–59 mmol/L as intermediate (lowered from 40–59) and ≤29 as normal, with diagnosis requiring clinical suspicion; no source read states a two-occasion rule. The lesson teaches the 2017 bands (register flag rv-sweat-cl-bands-2017).

Ch. 23 Hit 12 says Lewis-negative patients “cannot produce it at all”. Guo 2017 found undetectable CA 19-9 in Lewis-null participants, but Liu 2025 reviews reports of Lewis-negative cancer patients with CA 19-9 above 37 U/mL; Ballehaninna 2012 also notes the >100 U/mL specificity comes with lower sensitivity and that CA 19-9 has no role in screening. The lesson says “little or none” (register flag rv-ca199-lewis-not-absolute).
